case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress may insulate Federal Trade Commission Commissioners from at-will presidential removal (i.e., limit removal to “for cause”) consistent with Article II, and if not, what remedy follows from an unlawful removal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. II (the Executive Power and Take Care Clause framework, as applied through the President’s removal authority); the Federal Trade Commission Act’s “for cause” removal protections for FTC Commissioners (as interpreted through Humphrey’s Executor).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the President and Executive Branch) argue that Article II requires meaningful presidential control over officers exercising executive power, which in turn requires at-will removal (or at least prohibits the FTC’s for-cause tenure protection for principal officers). They contend that the FTC’s modern powers—rulemaking, enforcement, and adjudication with major economic/political consequences—are quintessentially executive in nature, so Humphrey’s Executor should be limited or overruled. They also press a remedial point that even if the removal was unlawful under existing statute/precedent, reinstatement/backpay-type relief is not automatically available (or is improper) absent a valid cause of action and proper equitable/mandamus prerequisites.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Slaughter and aligned parties) argue that Humphrey’s Executor squarely upholds for-cause removal limits for traditional multi-member independent commissions like the FTC, and that the Court should follow stare decisis rather than re-litigate the basic validity of independent agencies. They maintain that the FTC’s structure and functions fit within the long-accepted model of independent regulatory commissions, and that any expansions in authority do not convert the Commission into a purely executive department under presidential control. On remedy, they argue that an unlawful removal is legally ineffective and warrants declaratory/injunctive relief restoring the officer to her position because the governing statute and precedent make the removal invalid.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Article II critique is the strongest opposing argument: Humphrey’s Executor’s claim that the FTC exercises “no part of the executive power” is conceptually untenable given modern enforcement and rulemaking. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, Justice Kavanaugh’s “as-applied” approach supplies no administrable, text-rooted stopping rule and would effectively reopen Humphrey’s commission-by-commission, undermining reliance interests and our own statements in Seila Law and Collins that Humphrey’s remains a categorical carveout for traditional multimember commissions. Wiener, as Justice Sotomayor notes, further supports Congress’s ability to protect decisional independence in certain settings, though I do not need it to decide this case because Humphrey’s directly controls § 41. On remedy, I agree with Justice Alito that relief should be constrained by ordinary cause-of-action and equitable limits, but where a valid statutory restriction makes the removal unlawful, we should not announce a blanket bar on meaningful equitable relief.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis argument is the strongest point for Respondent, but it cannot control where the precedent rests on a constitutional mistake about the meaning of Article II—Humphrey’s Executor’s premise that the FTC exercises “no part of the executive power” is irreconcilable with the original public meaning of “[t]he executive Power” vested in a single President and with the FTC’s coercive enforcement authority. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett object that an “as-applied” approach lacks an administrable stopping rule, but that critique assumes we may continue applying an acknowledgedly erroneous constitutional carveout simply because it is old; original meaning supplies the stopping rule—principal officers exercising substantial executive power must remain subject to presidential control. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Wiener does not move me because it concerned a distinctly adjudicatory body and cannot justify insulating modern principal officers who combine rulemaking, prosecution, and adjudication in one commission. On remedy, I agree with Justices Alito and Gorsuch that the proper course is severance of the for-cause restriction, not judicially ordered reinstatement that would effectively enforce an unconstitutional tenure protection.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis argument is the most serious point for Respondent, especially given Seila Law’s language “preserving” Humphrey’s Executor for traditional multimember commissions. But as Justice Thomas explains, Humphrey’s turned on the constitutional premise that the FTC exercises “no part of the executive power,” a premise that cannot be squared with the modern FTC’s coercive enforcement and binding rulemaking; treating that outdated rationale as a categorical, time-immune carveout would entrench a constitutional mistake and dilute Article II accountability. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s administrability concern is real, yet an as-applied holding here is not a freewheeling “how executive” balancing test—it is the straightforward recognition that principal officers exercising core executive power cannot be insulated from at-will removal. On remedy, I continue to agree with Roberts that reinstatement/backpay should not be presumed; severance and restrained equitable relief avoid effectively enforcing an unconstitutional tenure protection.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest Article II point: Humphrey’s Executor’s claim that the FTC exercised “no part of the executive power” is descriptively untenable given modern enforcement and rulemaking. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that critique targets Humphrey’s reasoning, not its holding, and Seila Law and Collins repeatedly preserved Humphrey’s as a categorical carveout for the traditional multimember, bipartisan, staggered-term commission—an administrable line with enormous reliance interests. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed “as-applied” invalidation still lacks a workable stopping rule and would invite continuous litigation over shifting agency portfolios, destabilizing regulatory and adjudicatory regimes that materially protect vulnerable people. On remedy, I agree with Roberts that relief must respect ordinary equitable limits, but where a valid statute made the removal unlawful, meaningful declaratory/injunctive relief (including reinstatement when appropriate) remains the ordinary way to vindicate that legal constraint absent a demonstrated bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch forcefully argue that Humphrey’s Executor’s “no part of the executive power” rationale is incompatible with the FTC’s modern enforcement and rulemaking, but that is a critique of Humphrey’s reasoning, not a workable basis for disregarding its holding where Congress used unmistakable for-cause language in 15 U.S.C. § 41 and we have nearly a century of reliance. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Seila Law and Collins did not merely tolerate Humphrey’s; they repeatedly treated it as an extant categorical carveout for the traditional multimember commission model, which supplies the administrable rule that Justice Kavanaugh’s “as-applied” approach lacks. Kavanaugh’s proposal would require courts to recalibrate an agency’s constitutional status as its portfolio evolves, inviting the kind of functional grading our separation-of-powers cases typically resist and offering no text-based stopping rule beyond “substantial executive power.” On remedy, I remain aligned with Roberts and Justice Barrett that relief must be tethered to ordinary equitable limits, but where a valid statutory restriction rendered the removal unlawful, declaratory/injunctive relief can appropriately vindicate that constraint without converting every case into automatic reinstatement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s stare decisis point is the most substantial counterargument: Humphrey’s Executor is old, and Seila Law/Collins spoke of “preserving” it for traditional multimember commissions. But as Justice Thomas underscores, Humphrey’s rests on the constitutional premise that the FTC exercised “no part of the executive power,” and that premise cannot be squared with the modern FTC’s rulemaking, prosecution, and adjudication—functions that, under Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses, require presidential accountability through at-will removal of principal officers. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett’s administrability concern does not defeat that conclusion because the limiting principle is not a free-form functional balancing; it is whether principal officers are insulated from removal while exercising substantial executive power, a threshold plainly satisfied on this record. Wiener (as Justice Sotomayor notes) may justify independence for genuinely adjudicative bodies, but it cannot validate tenure protection for a hybrid commission combining policymaking and enforcement; the appropriate remedy is severance of the for-cause restriction with relief constrained by ordinary cause-of-action and equitable limits as Justice Alito emphasizes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis point is the strongest for Respondent, especially given Seila Law and Collins’s repeated descriptions of Humphrey’s Executor as a preserved carveout for “traditional” commissions. But I agree with Justice Thomas that Humphrey’s constitutional premise—that the FTC exercises “no part of the executive power”—cannot be squared with today’s FTC, which exercises core executive power through coercive enforcement and binding rulemaking; treating Humphrey’s as forever controlling despite that transformation would elevate an outdated characterization over Article II’s accountability structure. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right to worry about administrability, yet an as-applied approach keyed to specific exercises of executive power (enforcement actions and legislative rules) is more cabined than a free-form “how executive” balancing and avoids formally overruling Humphrey’s while preventing its reasoning from expanding to modern realities. On remedy, I remain aligned with Roberts and Justice Alito that reinstatement/backpay should not be presumed; declaratory relief and severance are the more restrained, institutionally cautious path.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to press the Article II tension: Humphrey’s Executor’s statement that the FTC exercises “no part of the executive power” is difficult to reconcile with modern enforcement and rulemaking, and Myers underscores the unitary Executive’s accountability logic. But under a textualist-originalist methodology that also takes stare decisis seriously in structural cases, Humphrey’s squarely upheld this exact § 41 for-cause protection for this exact Commission, and as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Seila Law and Collins treated that holding as a preserved categorical carveout for “traditional” multimember commissions rather than inviting reclassification based on evolving agency functions. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed “as-applied” approach, even if motivated by restraint, lacks a text-based limiting principle and would effectively reopen Humphrey’s through ad hoc functional gradations our separation-of-powers doctrine has struggled to administer. On remedy, I align with Roberts that, given a valid statutory constraint, equitable declaratory/injunctive relief can address an unlawful removal subject to ordinary limits, without announcing an automatic reinstatement rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that Humphrey’s Executor rests on an outdated description of the FTC as exercising “no part of the executive power,” which sits uneasily with modern enforcement and rulemaking. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Seila Law and Collins did not merely tolerate Humphrey’s—they reaffirmed it as a categorical carveout for the traditional multimember commission structure, and I am not persuaded we should convert that settled rule into Justice Kavanaugh’s shifting “as-applied” inquiry that would invite commission-by-commission functional relitigation with no stable stopping rule. Even accepting the Article II accountability concern, stare decisis carries particular weight here because the holding is administrable (for-cause protection for a classic FTC-style multimember body) and reliance interests are profound, while Petitioners have not shown the regime is unworkable. On remedy, I agree with Roberts that equitable limits and cause-of-action principles matter, but I do not accept Justice Alito’s suggestion that reinstatement-type relief is categorically improper where a valid statutory constraint was violated; ordinary declaratory/injunctive relief remains available absent a specific equitable bar.

John Roberts.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) directly upheld the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, and this case presents the same institutional structure (a multimember commission) Congress chose for the FTC under 15 U.S.C. § 41. Given stare decisis and the Court’s repeated treatment of Humphrey’s as controlling for traditional independent commissions (even while declining to extend it to novel arrangements in Seila Law), the narrowest, legitimacy-preserving course is to reaffirm Humphrey’s rather than overrule it based on asserted changes in the FTC’s modern portfolio. On remedy, even assuming an Article II violation were found, the Court should proceed cautiously and avoid an automatic reinstatement rule absent a clear cause of action and equitable entitlement; but because the for-cause protection is valid under Humphrey’s, the removal is unlawful under the statute and declaratory/injunctive relief restoring the status quo is appropriate on these facts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests “[t]he executive Power” in a single President, and the Take Care Clause presupposes presidential control over those who execute federal law; that original allocation is incompatible with Congress granting principal officers exercising executive power—like FTC Commissioners who engage in enforcement, rulemaking, and executive adjudication—tenure protection limiting removal to “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance.” Myers v. United States recognized the President’s removal power over executive officers as inherent in Article II and repeatedly described it as “unrestricted,” and later decisions such as Seila Law confirm that Humphrey’s Executor’s premise (that the FTC exercised “no part of the executive power”) was at best a narrow, historically contingent rationale that cannot justify modern insulation of an agency wielding substantial executive authority. To the extent Humphrey’s Executor authorizes for-cause limits for such executive officers, it is irreconcilable with the Constitution’s text and structure and should be overruled or confined to non-executive functions. Because the statutory removal restriction is unconstitutional, the attempted “for-cause” constraint cannot supply a basis to invalidate the President’s removal; at minimum, no reinstatement follows from enforcing an unconstitutional tenure protection.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article II vests the Executive Power in the President and requires that he be able to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” which in practical terms demands meaningful presidential control over principal officers who wield substantial executive authority; the FTC’s modern rulemaking and enforcement powers look far more like core executive power than the “quasi-legislative”/“quasi-judicial” description relied on in Humphrey’s Executor. Although Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) upheld for-cause protection for FTC Commissioners, its rationale is difficult to square with the Constitution’s accountability structure where the President must be able to supervise and, when necessary, remove those executing federal law. As a remedy, even assuming a statutory violation, reinstatement/backpay does not follow automatically: under Marbury v. Madison (1803) a remedy depends on a valid cause of action and proper equitable prerequisites, and courts should hesitate to impose coercive relief that entrenches an unconstitutional removal restriction. Accordingly, I would hold the for-cause limitation unconstitutional as applied to principal officers exercising significant executive power and reject automatic reinstatement absent a clear remedial authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) remains controlling precedent squarely upholding Congress’s decision in the FTC Act to limit presidential removal of FTC Commissioners to “for cause,” and this Court should not destabilize the long-settled independence of multi-member commissions through dicta in later cases like Seila Law or Morrison. Whatever the modern FTC’s mix of rulemaking, enforcement, and adjudication, Wiener v. United States (1958) reinforces that Congress may structure adjudicatory and regulatory bodies to protect decisional independence where the statute reflects that design, and stare decisis carries special weight for institutional arrangements relied on across government. Because the statute makes removal without cause unlawful, the removal is legally ineffective; consistent with Marbury v. Madison (1803), courts must provide a meaningful remedy, and declaratory and injunctive relief restoring the Commissioner is an appropriate, practical means to vindicate statutory tenure protections and preserve fair, impartial administration—especially where politically motivated removals can undermine enforcement that protects consumers and other vulnerable populations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor squarely sustained the FTC Act’s for-cause removal restriction for FTC Commissioners, characterizing the Commission as a multimember body performing quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions, and this Court has repeatedly left that framework intact even while narrowing other removal limits in cases like Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law. Whatever doubts Seila Law expressed about Humphrey’s reasoning, it expressly preserved Humphrey’s Executor as governing precedent for the “traditional independent agency” model, and the FTC still fits that statutory structure (15 U.S.C. § 41). Overruling or effectively gutting Humphrey’s would unsettle a long-settled congressional design choice and create serious workability problems across similarly structured commissions, with no clear textual stopping rule in Article II for distinguishing permissible from impermissible insulation short of rejecting the category wholesale. On remedy, if the removal violated the for-cause statute as construed in Humphrey’s, the removal is unlawful and declaratory/injunctive relief restoring the Commissioner is the ordinary equitable consequence absent some independent bar, consistent with Marbury’s premise that legal rights have legal remedies.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting Clause and Take Care Clause assign the executive power to a single President, and the historical understanding reflected in Myers v. United States recognizes removal as an incident of that power; Congress’s only express after-the-fact check is impeachment. Humphrey’s Executor v. United States approved for-cause tenure for FTC Commissioners by invoking “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial” labels, but those labels do not fit comfortably with the FTC’s modern exercise of core executive functions—rulemaking, enforcement, and adjudication—carried out by principal officers who are not meaningfully accountable to the President. Because such insulation severs the Madisonian “chain of dependence” central to separation of powers, I would hold the FTC Act’s for-cause protection unconstitutional as applied and sever it, leaving the Commission to operate with at-will presidential removal; any additional relief like reinstatement or backpay would require an independent cause of action and satisfy ordinary equitable limits rather than follow automatically from the constitutional violation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) upheld for-cause removal for FTC Commissioners based on the premise that the FTC was predominantly “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial,” but that description was tied to the Commission’s then-understood, more limited role and cannot be reflexively extended to an FTC that today exercises substantial executive power through enforcement, adjudication, and expansive rulemaking. Under Article II’s Executive Power and Take Care Clause framework, Congress may not substantially dilute presidential accountability over principal officers performing core executive functions, and the FTC’s combination of breadth and coercive authority makes the traditional Humphrey’s model difficult to justify on workability and accountability grounds. Consistent with judicial restraint and institutional concerns, the proper course is to hold the FTC Act’s “for cause” restriction (15 U.S.C. § 41) unconstitutional as applied and sever it, rather than dismantling the agency. On remedy, I would avoid a broad reinstatement rule and instead require the usual showing of a valid cause of action and equitable prerequisites, consistent with Marbury v. Madison’s distinction between legal right and remedial entitlement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTC Act provides Commissioners may be removed only for "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office," 15 U.S.C. § 41, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) held that this precise for-cause protection for the FTC is consistent with Article II given the Commission’s multi-member structure and its mix of "quasi-legislative" and "quasi-judicial" functions. While later decisions (Free Enterprise Fund, Seila Law, Collins) have emphasized presidential accountability and limited certain removal restrictions, they have repeatedly left Humphrey’s Executor "in place" for traditional multi-member independent commissions rather than overruling it. Applying methodological consistency and stare decisis, I would adhere to Humphrey’s Executor on the constitutionality question in this case; any debate about the FTC’s modern powers is better addressed through narrower future litigation or legislative change rather than overruling a nearly century-old precedent. Given that the statute makes an at-will removal legally unauthorized, declaratory and injunctive relief treating the removal as unlawful is an appropriate remedy on ordinary equitable principles (cf. Marbury) where a plaintiff establishes a legal right and a court can afford effective relief.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) squarely upheld the FTC Act’s “for cause” removal protection for FTC Commissioners, characterizing the Commission as a multimember body performing “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial” functions, and that basic structural holding has been left intact rather than repudiated by later Article II removal cases. Given the reliance interests built around independent commissions and the absence of a clear administrable alternative, stare decisis in a constitutional-structure case still counsels against overruling Humphrey’s absent a showing that the regime is unworkable, and the record here does not show that. On remedy, consistent with Marbury v. Madison (1803) and ordinary equitable principles, a removal that violates the FTC Act’s for-cause limitation is unlawful and warrants declaratory/injunctive relief restoring the officer’s status unless the government identifies a concrete barrier (e.g., lack of cause of action or equitable prerequisites) that would make reinstatement impracticable in this context. The practical consequences of allowing at-will removals here—politicizing adjudicatory/enforcement functions and destabilizing regulatory continuity—also weigh against adopting petitioners’ sweeping Article II theory.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Constitution permits Congress to insulate Federal Trade Commission Commissioners from at-will presidential removal (and, if the removal was unlawful, what the proper judicial remedy is).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution Article II (Vesting Clause/Take Care Clause and the implied presidential removal power) and the Federal Trade Commission Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the President and Executive Branch officials) argue that FTC Commissioners exercise substantial executive power and therefore must remain accountable to the President through at-will removal; they contend Humphrey’s Executor should be overruled or narrowed because it wrongly permits Congress to create powerful, politically unaccountable independent agencies, and they further suggest limits on the availability of reinstatement-type relief even if a statutory violation is found.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (including the removed FTC Commissioner) argue that the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection controls; under Humphrey’s Executor (and related decisions), the FTC is a traditional independent agency whose commissioners may not be removed at will, so the attempted removal was unlawful and legally ineffective, and courts can provide declaratory/injunctive relief (including treating the officer as remaining in office) to remedy the violation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that Humphrey’s Executor rests on an analytically weak “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” distinction and is hard to justify on originalist premises, but that critique does not erase that Humphrey’s squarely upheld this very tenure scheme for this very agency—and Seila Law and Collins expressly said they were not disturbing it, which substantially strengthens stare decisis and institutional legitimacy concerns. Justice Kavanaugh’s effort to “confine” Humphrey’s based on the FTC’s modern enforcement footprint directly engages the Article II worry, yet it fails my minimalism test because it offers no administrable limiting principle and invites case-by-case reclassification of independent agencies that our recent decisions purported to leave undisturbed. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Free Enterprise Fund/Seila Law’s accountability framework underscores the structural concern, but those cases themselves drew a line that preserved traditional multimember commissions, and crossing it here would functionally overrule Humphrey’s under another name. Collins matters chiefly on remedy: even assuming a statutory violation under Humphrey’s, relief should be tailored to concrete prospective harm rather than broad reinstatement or undoing past actions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is that Humphrey’s Executor squarely upheld this very statutory scheme and that stare decisis should control; but under an originalist account of Article II, precedent that dilutes the President’s executive power and the Take Care duty cannot be perpetuated merely by longevity, especially when Humphrey’s rests on the unstable “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” distinction. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan emphasize that Seila Law and Collins purported to preserve Humphrey’s; I view those statements as describing existing doctrine, not supplying an original-meaning justification for insulating principal officers who wield substantial enforcement authority. Marbury’s remedial principle does not authorize reinstatement-type relief that would itself entrench an unconstitutional tenure protection and interfere with the President’s constitutionally required supervision, a concern Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch correctly frame as a structural limit on equitable relief. Accordingly, I would hold the for-cause restriction unconstitutional (and Humphrey’s overruled or at least confined beyond recognition as applied to the FTC’s core executive functions), rendering the removal effective and precluding compelled reinstatement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis point is the most serious obstacle, especially given Seila Law and Collins’s statements that they were not “disturbing” Humphrey’s Executor; but I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that those passages are best read as descriptive of then-existing doctrine, not as an entrenchment of Humphrey’s rationale against future application where the agency’s functions have plainly evolved. Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson warn that an as-applied approach invites line-drawing, yet that concern cannot justify maintaining a rule that lets Congress evade Article II accountability by assigning core enforcement power to multimember bodies; here, the FTC’s investigative/prosecutorial posture is not marginal but central, making the constitutional problem concrete rather than speculative. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Wiener does not move me because Wiener involved a uniquely adjudicatory body designed for decisional independence, whereas the FTC is a standing regulator and enforcer, so the democratic-accountability interest is paramount. On remedy, Collins supports recognizing a constitutional violation while requiring a showing of harm before undoing agency action, which answers Roberts’s and Jackson’s concern about disruption without converting removal defects into automatic reinstatement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest Article II case by attacking Humphrey’s Executor’s “quasi-” rationale as analytically unstable and mismatched to the FTC’s modern enforcement posture, but that critique targets reasoning, not the controlling holding that squarely upheld this very multimember for-cause scheme—one Seila Law and Collins expressly said they were not unsettling. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed “as-applied confinement” supplies no administrable limiting principle and would invite pervasive, strategic relitigation across the independent-agency landscape, effectively overruling Humphrey’s in practice while disclaiming it in name. On remedy, Collins supports tailoring backward-looking relief to demonstrated harm, but it does not justify denying meaningful prospective relief for the concrete, ongoing injury of unlawful displacement from office; Marbury’s core remedial principle supports declaratory/injunctive relief to halt an ongoing statutory violation without unraveling past agency actions. Under a pragmatic, stability- and fairness-focused approach attentive to institutional legitimacy and real-world consequences, I would adhere to settled precedent and enforce Congress’s for-cause protection here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point for the petitioner: that we can “confine” Humphrey’s Executor because the modern FTC exercises substantial enforcement power, and that Free Enterprise Fund/Seila Law’s accountability framework makes the inquiry administrable. But as Chief Justice Roberts argues, that move lacks a workable limiting principle because it turns Seila Law and Collins’s express preservation of Humphrey’s for traditional multimember commissions into an invitation for pervasive, agency-by-agency reclassification—effectively overruling Humphrey’s in the very setting it addressed. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s originalist critique exposes weaknesses in Humphrey’s reasoning, yet under my pragmatic textualist approach and stare decisis, the controlling holding plus our recent reliance language counsel applying the for-cause standard as written here, while taking Collins seriously on remedy by requiring concrete harm and tailoring relief rather than reflexively undoing agency action. Wiener does not change the outcome for me; if anything, it underscores that our doctrine has long accepted some tenure protection in adjudicatory-leaning contexts, and the doctrinally coherent path is to apply Humphrey’s rather than create a modernization test with destabilizing spillover effects.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s stare decisis point—that Humphrey’s Executor involved the same agency and that Seila Law/Collins said they were not “disturbing” it—is the most serious obstacle, but it does not defeat an Article II analysis grounded in text and structure. As Justice Thomas explains, Humphrey’s rests on the analytically unstable premise that the FTC does not exercise executive power; whatever the label in 1935, today’s FTC wields quintessentially executive authority through investigation, prosecution, and binding adjudication, and Congress cannot insulate that power from presidential supervision without violating the Vesting and Take Care Clauses. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern is real, yet the inquiry is not free-form “how executive” an agency feels; it turns on objective, statutory features of power Congress has conferred—an approach already required by Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law when assessing whether tenure protections meaningfully impair accountability. On remedy, Collins reinforces that we should sever the for-cause restriction as applied and avoid reinstatement-type relief that would itself entrench the constitutional defect.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is that Humphrey’s Executor involved this very agency and that Seila Law/Collins included “preservation” language, and I agree we must avoid a freewheeling, case-by-case inquiry that would undermine stability. But I think Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson overread those preservation statements as freezing Humphrey’s irrespective of its own factual predicates; an institutionalist stare decisis approach can confine a precedent to the conditions on which it rested, and Humphrey’s central premise—that the FTC did not exercise substantial executive power—fits poorly with the FTC’s modern investigative and prosecutorial enforcement posture emphasized by Justice Alito. That said, Roberts is right on administrability concerns, so any holding should be narrowly tied to objective statutory features of authority (not agency “evolution” writ large) and accompanied by Collins-style remedial restraint—severance/prospective relief rather than reinstatement-like decrees that entrench the tenure protection. On that narrower path, I remain persuaded the Article II accountability problem is acute enough here to warrant relief for the petitioner without announcing a sweeping rule against all multimember commissions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis argument is the most serious obstacle: Humphrey’s Executor involved the same agency and materially similar tenure language, and Seila Law/Collins said they were not "disturbing" it. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, those preservation statements describe the doctrinal landscape rather than justify—on Article II’s text and original public meaning—insulating principal officers who today exercise substantial executive enforcement and adjudicatory power, and Humphrey’s "quasi-" framework is too indeterminate to serve as a stable constitutional rule. I agree with Justice Kagan that administrability matters, yet the inquiry here can be anchored to objective statutory authorities and the FTC’s core functions, not fluctuating policy emphases, making an as-applied holding workable. Collins remains central on remedy: even if the restriction is unconstitutional, relief should be tailored to concrete harm rather than automatic reinstatement, which answers the respondents’ claim that invalidation necessarily entails sweeping remedial consequences.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that confining Humphrey’s Executor to its “historical predicates” is an institutionally modest move, but in this case that move collapses into overruling in practice: the precedent upheld this very agency and statutory tenure protection, and modernizing it via an as-applied “how executive is it now” inquiry lacks a principled, administrable stopping point and would predictably destabilize reliance interests across the independent-agency landscape. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Seila Law and Collins did more than offer a passing description—they structured the doctrine around preserving Humphrey’s for traditional multimember commissions, and it would be procedurally unfair to invite regulated parties and displaced officers into pervasive litigation over agency “executiveness” absent a clear rule. Justice Thomas’s originalist critique highlights Humphrey’s shaky rationale, but under my pragmatic stare decisis approach the holding remains controlling here, and Collins is best read to cabin remedies to concrete harm without stripping courts of power to provide workable prospective relief for an ongoing unlawful removal. I therefore would adhere to Humphrey’s Executor on the merits and address remedy narrowly rather than rewriting Article II doctrine through an unstable, case-by-case test.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTC Act expressly limits removal of Commissioners to “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office,” and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) squarely upheld that for-cause protection for the FTC as an independent, multi-member commission exercising rulemaking and adjudicatory functions distinct from purely executive officers governed by Myers. Whatever the force of broader Article II arguments, principles of stare decisis and institutional legitimacy counsel against overruling or substantially narrowing Humphrey’s Executor in a case that presents the same agency and materially the same statutory structure, particularly given Congress’s long reliance on that settlement. If the removal violated the statute (and thus was unlawful), the proper remedy is prospective declaratory and injunctive relief recognizing the statutory limitation, consistent with Marbury v. Madison’s premise that courts must provide a remedy for legal wrongs while avoiding unnecessary disruption beyond what is needed to enforce the governing law. A narrow disposition on precedent and statutory application resolves the case without announcing a sweeping rule about all independent agencies or all forms of for-cause tenure protections.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses assign the executive power—and the responsibility to ensure faithful execution of the laws—to the President, which necessarily implies authority to supervise and, when necessary, remove principal executive officers who wield substantial enforcement power. FTC Commissioners are principal officers exercising core executive power, and Congress’s for-cause removal restriction in the FTC Act therefore impermissibly dilutes presidential accountability and creates an unaccountable executive apparatus inconsistent with the Constitution’s original public meaning. Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) rests on an untenable “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” distinction and should be overruled or at least confined so it cannot sustain removal protections for modern agencies exercising broad executive authority. Because the restriction is unconstitutional, the attempted at-will removal is effective, and the proper remedy is to deny reinstatement-type relief that would negate the President’s constitutionally required control over executive officers.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses presuppose that the President must be able to supervise and control the execution of federal law, and that supervision is defeated if principal officers exercising substantial executive power are insulated from at-will removal. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) said about the FTC as “quasi-legislative” or “quasi-judicial,” the modern FTC’s core functions—rulemaking, enforcement actions, and administrative adjudication—are executive in character, and later decisions (e.g., Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB and Seila Law LLC v. CFPB) have recognized that removal restrictions cannot be allowed to sever democratic accountability in the Executive Branch. Consistent with those cases’ emphasis on the President’s ability to oversee execution of the laws, the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for Commissioners is unconstitutional as applied to principal officers heading an agency wielding broad enforcement authority, and Humphrey’s Executor should be narrowed to its historical context at minimum. As for remedy, under Collins v. Yellen the appropriate course is to set aside actions only upon a showing of harm while recognizing that the removal restriction itself is invalid; courts need not order reinstatement as an automatic remedy for a separation-of-powers violation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for Commissioners is directly upheld by Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935), which sustained Congress’s choice to structure the FTC as a multimember independent commission insulated from at-will presidential removal, and nothing in Article II compels overruling that settled framework here. Our more recent cases—Free Enterprise Fund, Seila Law, and Collins—carefully distinguished and preserved Humphrey’s Executor for traditional multimember independent agencies, while striking down only additional layers of insulation or the novel single-director model. Because the attempted at-will removal violated the FTC Act and thus was unlawful, courts may provide effective equitable relief under Marbury v. Madison, including declaratory and injunctive relief recognizing the Commissioner’s continuing entitlement to office, especially to prevent concrete harms to the agency’s independence and to the public the FTC protects.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) squarely upheld the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, distinguishing the Commission’s mixed functions and allowing Congress to structure a multimember, bipartisan expert body insulated from at-will removal. Whatever later cases (e.g., Seila Law) have said about particular agency designs, they preserved Humphrey’s Executor’s core holding for traditional multi-member commissions, and Wiener v. United States (1958) reinforces that when Congress creates adjudicatory or quasi-judicial bodies, removal limits can be implied or sustained to protect decisional independence. Given that Congress has expressly provided for-cause protection in the FTC Act and this Court has repeatedly treated that arrangement as constitutionally permissible, I would not overrule Humphrey’s Executor absent a clearer constitutional necessity; the appropriate remedy for an unlawful at-will removal is declaratory/injunctive relief recognizing the statutory violation rather than attempting to constitutionalize broad limits on equitable remedies beyond what is needed to resolve this case. That narrower course respects Article II while preserving statutory coherence and workability for longstanding administrative structures.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses assign the executive power to the President, and a meaningful share of that power is the ability to supervise those who execute federal law through at-will removal, absent a historically grounded exception. Humphrey’s Executor’s “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” label has proven unstable, and later decisions have treated limits on presidential control as narrow and exceptional rather than the default—especially where officials exercise substantial executive authority. The FTC today wields core executive power through investigation, enforcement, and binding adjudication under the FTC Act, and Congress may not convert principal executive officers into politically unaccountable actors by for-cause tenure. Consistent with Seila Law and Free Enterprise Fund, the for-cause restriction is unconstitutional as applied to FTC Commissioners, and the proper remedy is severance of the offending tenure protection rather than judicially compelled “reinstatement” that would further intrude on Article II supervision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses require meaningful presidential control over officers who exercise substantial executive power, and the FTC’s modern enforcement and regulatory authority under 15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(2) is quintessentially executive in operation. Under Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, Humphrey’s Executor is best read narrowly as permitting for-cause protection only for a multimember, bipartisan expert commission that was understood to perform predominantly quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial functions and not to wield substantial executive power; that rationale does not comfortably fit the FTC as it functions today. Respecting precedent and institutional stability, I would not overrule Humphrey’s Executor outright, but would confine it to its historical premises and hold the FTC Act’s for-cause protection unconstitutional as applied to Commissioners exercising significant executive enforcement authority. If the removal restriction is invalid, the proper remedy is to set it aside rather than to mandate reinstatement, consistent with judicial restraint and separation-of-powers limits on coercive equitable relief against the President.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses vest the executive power in the President and presuppose sufficient supervisory control, including removal, over officers who exercise executive authority. Humphrey’s Executor upheld for-cause protection for FTC Commissioners on the premise that the FTC’s functions were “neither political nor executive,” but subsequent decisions have treated that rationale as limited and have emphasized that removal restrictions are constitutionally suspect when they impede presidential control over executive power. See Seila Law LLC v. CFPB and Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (rejecting structures that dilute accountability), and Collins v. Yellen (recognizing a constitutional violation from an unlawful removal restriction while tailoring remedies to concrete harm). Because the FTC exercises substantial executive power through enforcement, rulemaking, and adjudication, Congress may not insulate its Commissioners from at-will removal in a manner that materially diminishes presidential accountability.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) squarely upheld the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, reasoning that the Commission was structured as a multimember, bipartisan body performing “predominantly quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative” functions and thus not subject to unrestricted at-will presidential removal under Article II. Whatever the modern debate about the FTC’s role, stare decisis and procedural fairness counsel against overruling that entrenched precedent absent a clear showing that the constitutional framework has become unworkable, and the record here does not justify destabilizing a longstanding statutory arrangement governing an entire category of “traditional independent agencies.” If the attempted removal violated the FTC Act’s for-cause standard, courts may provide declaratory and injunctive relief to remedy the unlawful action consistent with Marbury v. Madison’s principle that where there is a legal right, there must be a legal remedy. Practical consequences also cut against narrowing judicial remedies in a way that would leave unlawfully removed officers without meaningful recourse and would invite evasion of statutory constraints.
